reviewer: Independent AI reviewer A; did not write these eight articles
scope: Read all eight C drafts, their complete Rust bins, shared library, Cargo pins and README. Edited only the eight MDX files and this record. No local builds, tests, compiler, formatter, native connections or other runtime workloads.
style_standard: Plain natural English for developers including non-native readers. Reject vague abstractions, invented incidents, canned lessons and repeated CI/publishing narration. No certification of human authorship or a writer's native language.
overall_verdict: Revise rather than accept the original prose unchanged. The concrete problems and bounded examples are useful; remove workflow narration, narrow the plan title and replace vague advice with actual checks. All dates and draft/review holds remain unchanged. This review grants no publication approval.
verification_status: Code fences were compared as text with the originals and preserved byte for byte. Native SQL Server, Oracle and Db2 service runs are separate from compilation and pure Rust tests; no unobserved runtime result is claimed. Coordinator owns remote CI and native-service evidence.
word_count_method: Whitespace-separated reader tokens containing an ASCII letter or digit after removing frontmatter, fenced code and Markdown URL destinations. Headings and inline identifiers retained. Lightweight text inspection only.

changes.rejected_passage: An equality predicate does not automatically become a null test because a bound parameter is absent. If the report wants rows without a label, use the query branch designed to test absence. If it wants rows with a particular label, bind that label in the ordinary equality query.
changes.replacement: A predicate such as `label = :1` does not become a null test when the bound value is null. Oracle evaluates that comparison as unknown, so a `WHERE` clause does not select the row. To find rows without a label, use `label IS NULL`. To find a particular label, bind it in the equality query. The [null comparison rules](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/sqlrf/Nulls.html) explain the difference.
changes.reason: Replace an evasive instruction with the actual SQL predicate and result.

changes.rejected_passage: Precision and scale matter separately. Precision concerns the decimal digits a declaration allows. Scale controls the position of the decimal point. A monetary amount with a nonzero scale is not simply a bigger integer; it needs an agreed decimal representation and rounding policy.
changes.replacement: Precision and scale matter separately. For example, `NUMBER(12,2)` allows twelve significant decimal digits, with two places after the decimal point. It is not the same field as `NUMBER(12,0)`. If the column stores money, decide which decimal representation and rounding rules the application must preserve before choosing a Rust type.
changes.reason: Use a concrete declaration to explain precision and scale.

changes.rejected_passage: These examples are small enough for the text form to remain ordinary integral decimal digits. If the actual schema allows much larger magnitudes, fractional scales, or a format that produces an exponent, choose and test a representation that supports those cases. A parser written for this `NUMBER(38,0)` contract should reject them rather than guess.
changes.replacement: The three integers need at most thirty-eight digits. Oracle's [`TM9` format](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/sqlrf/Format-Models.html) switches to scientific notation only when the output would exceed 64 characters, so these values should remain ordinary decimal digits. An unconstrained `NUMBER` or a fractional value needs a separate formatting and parsing decision. The helper here rejects fractions and exponents rather than guessing what they mean.
changes.reason: Explain why TM9 is suitable for these selected values with a direct primary reference.

changes.rejected_passage: For this integral contract, a Rust `i128` can hold all signed values with up to thirty-eight decimal digits. The fixture's helper accepts only that bounded integer syntax and then uses a checked conversion if a caller still requires `i64`. Its feature-free tests cover the boundary and reject fractions, exponents, and other unsupported forms.
changes.replacement: For these integral values, a Rust `i128` can hold every signed value with up to thirty-eight decimal digits. The helper accepts digits with an optional leading minus sign, then uses a checked conversion if a caller still requires `i64`. Its Rust tests cover the boundary and reject fractions, exponents, and other unsupported forms.
changes.reason: Replace contract and feature terminology with the accepted syntax and tests.

changes.rejected_passage: The database assertions remain pending until a real Oracle Client and service run them in CI. changes.replacement: The <ArticleLink slug="adding-rust-to-a-system-that-already-uses-oracle">shared Oracle connection helper</ArticleLink> checks the declared exact server version and requires Client 18.1 or later because it sets a call timeout.
